body:
```suggestion
				Delays execution of the current thread by [param msec] milliseconds with higher precision. [param msec] must be greater than or equal to [code]0[/code]. Otherwise, [method precise_delay_msec] does nothing and prints an error message.
				Compared to [method delay_msec], [method precise_delay_msec] is more precise at low sleep intervals at the cost of higher CPU utilization. [method precise_delay_msec] should be preferred in scenarios where stability over time is preferred, e.g. for frame pacing.
				[b]Note:[/b] [method precise_delay_msec] is a [i]blocking[/i] way to delay code execution. To delay code execution in a non-blocking way, you may use [method SceneTree.create_timer]. Awaiting with [SceneTreeTimer] delays the execution of code placed below the [code]await[/code] without affecting the rest of the project (or editor, for [EditorPlugin]s and [EditorScript]s).
				[b]Note:[/b] When [method precise_delay_msec] is called on the main thread, it will freeze the project and will prevent it from redrawing and registering input until the delay has passed. When using [method precise_delay_msec] as part of an [EditorPlugin] or [EditorScript], it will freeze the editor but won't freeze the project if it is currently running (since the project is an independent child process).
```

Given this is only used to block the main thread to pause between frames, do these need to be thread local?
Do we need all these logic if we need the sleep is always going to be sub 1 second?
The units are in microseconds so it is necessary.
They can be static instead. I was assuming this function could be called by different threads at once, but if only the main thread calls it static is fine too.

A simple busy wait would burn more CPU cycles than necessary. You need to sleep coarsely first, and then spin the rest of the time. For the coarse sleep, you would need to change the logic based on platform.
Let's say frame time is 19ms/frame, and you want to limit to 30FPS (33.33ms). That means you would end up spinning 14.33ms on the main thread.
Fixed!
Can't the function assume some upper bound? E.g. sleep 1 or 2 ms less than what it should and busy wait only that 1 or 2 ms? Do we have any data on how better/worse that would perform?
Or... given the current implementation runs based on estimates, why does the code that runs the estimates need to be platform-dependent?

I don't think so. On macOS, I see errors going up to several milliseconds, and this is just on one machine. Based on OS and hardware, I don't think we can assume a single upper bound unless we make it so conservative that we just end up wasting cycles spinning.
Windows explicitly calls timeBeginPeriod(1), which gives a definite upper bound.
Thanks for the suggestion! I can make that part of a separate PR to improve readability. This PR just moves the function so all platforms can access it.

So, given this is going to be hardware dependent, should we instead use the estimate logic everywhere (and just move it inside `add_frame_delay` instead of creating a dedicated function in each platform)?

We could do that, but I think it would be better on Windows to avoid the estimate tracking. Should I move the logic for Windows/Unix into one function and add an #if branch? I can imagine some platforms could have quirks with the delay. But reimplementing add_frame_delay for each platform with minor changes seems like too much code duplication, which is why the current method uses a virtual function to isolate per platform logic.

Another benefit is having a separate precise function is it could be reused in the future for any code that requires high precision.
Are we sure that on windows we don't need the estimation? I.e. do we know for sure that on windows there's not going to be differences depending on the hardware we are running on?

Yes, timeBeginPeriod(1) will guarantee us an upper bound that can be used instead of using estimation to best predict the upper bound 😊

Unix does not expose a similar API so we need to estimate the upper bound on the fly.

Well, according to [this](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/synchapi/nf-synchapi-sleep#remarks) and [this](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/timeapi/nf-timeapi-timebeginperiod), `timeBeginPeriod(1)` does not guarantee that the sleep will indeed result in that resolution (should we check `timeGetDevCaps` too maybe?), the same way Unix [`clock_getres`](https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/000095399/functions/clock_getres.html) will tell you the resolution of the MONOTONIC clock, but also won't guarantee that `sleep` time (i.e. that would be a lower bound).

Within the Windows logic of precise_delay_usec, Sleep is called only with 1ms increments (note / 1000). Calling timeBeginPeriod(1) (assuming the call succeeds) should sent the resolution to 1ms. Issues would only occur if timeBeginPeriod(1) did not succeed if a 1ms resolution is not supported.
What we can do to be 100% correct is call timeBeginPeriod with lowest number supported by device, and adjust the delay function accordingly.
